title: The same winners, year after year, department by department
question: How much of each department’s outside spending goes to its ten largest payees, how many of them are the same names as in fiscal 2019, and how much reaches payees that are new?
finding: Across all departments the ten largest payees of each took 63% of outside spending in fiscal 2019 and 57% in fiscal 2026. On average 3.8 of a department’s ten were still the 2019 names in 2026, and those 2019 names received 33% of the 2026 money; payees new to their department took 4.4%. Of 30 departments compared, the circle is most closed at Adult Probation (90% of fiscal 2026 money to its 2019 top ten; 6 of ten names unchanged), Assessor - Recorder (77%) and City Attorney (76%); it is most open at Port (2%), Fire Department (6%), Controller (10%).
how: Outside spending is payments for goods, services, grants and capital work to parties that are not public bodies, from the Controller’s payment file for fiscal 2019 to 2026 (a fiscal year runs July to June). Each payment is counted in the year its voucher was issued, which is read from the voucher number and not from the year the file lists it under. For each department and year the ten payees paid most are found. "Same names" counts how many of the 2026 ten were also in the 2019 ten. "Held" is the share of the department’s 2026 money paid to its 2019 top ten. A payee is new to a department in the first year that department pays it; the test looks back to fiscal 2017, a payee to whom the department issued a payment in fiscal 2018 or earlier, filed under a later year, is not new, and the average covers fiscal 2020 to 2026. Departments with under $50 million over the eight years, or fewer than 40 payees in any year, are left out of the ranking but counted in the citywide figures. Ranked by "held".
limits: Incumbents can also keep winning where the service is specialised, the same clients need continuity of care, few providers qualify, or one multi-year contract spans the whole period. A department that buys a specialised service (elections equipment, property-tax software, treatment beds) has few possible suppliers, and a department that builds things changes contractors when projects end, so capital departments look open and service departments look closed for reasons that have nothing to do with favour. Payees are matched by name: a renamed payee counts as a new one. The record that would settle a closed circle is the solicitation file for each of the ten: how many bids came in and how they were scored. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. The $992.6 million of outside spending that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier is in none of the figures here; it is used only to tell that a payee is not new.
